_meta.description: The 40 inventive principles of TRIZ. Names follow the usual English numbering; sub-principles and examples are this project's own wording.

principles.name: Segmentation
subprinciples: Split an object into independent parts.
Make the object easy to take apart and put back together.
Increase how finely the object is divided.

examples.engineering: Modular furniture that ships flat and bolts together.
examples.software: Split a monolith into services that deploy on their own.
examples.business: Split customers into segments with their own offers.
examples.everyday: Cut a big chore into 15-minute pieces.

principles.name: Taking out
subprinciples: Remove the part or property that causes trouble.
Pull out only the part or property you actually need.

examples.engineering: Put a noisy compressor outside the building.
examples.software: Move slow work out of the request path into a background job.
examples.business: Outsource a non-core task such as payroll.
examples.everyday: Leave the phone in another room while you work.

principles.name: Local quality
subprinciples: Change a uniform structure or environment into a non-uniform one.
Let each part of an object do a different job.
Put each part in the conditions that suit it best.

examples.engineering: A hammer with a hard face and a shock-absorbing handle.
examples.software: Cache hot data in memory and keep cold data on cheap storage.
examples.business: Price differently by region.
examples.everyday: A desk with a standing area and a sitting area.

principles.name: Asymmetry
subprinciples: Replace a symmetric form with an asymmetric one.
If it is already asymmetric, make it more so.

examples.engineering: A keyed plug that only fits one way.
examples.software: Give reads many replicas and writes one primary.
examples.business: Spend more on the few accounts that bring most revenue.
examples.everyday: An offset handle on a mug so it does not tip.

principles.name: Merging
subprinciples: Bring together identical or related objects, or objects meant for related operations.
Make operations run at the same time or next to each other.

examples.engineering: Twin-blade razors.
examples.software: Batch many small writes into one request.
examples.business: Combine two teams that hand work to each other all day.
examples.everyday: Cook a week of lunches in one session.

principles.name: Universality
subprinciples: Let one object do several jobs so other objects are no longer needed.

examples.engineering: A sofa that turns into a bed.
examples.software: One config file that drives build, test and deploy.
examples.business: Staff who handle both sales and support for small clients.
examples.everyday: A phone that is also a camera, map and wallet.

principles.name: Nested doll
subprinciples: Put one object inside another, and that one inside a third.
Let one part pass through a cavity in another.

examples.engineering: Telescopic antennas; stacking cups.
examples.software: Containers inside VMs; nested layouts in a UI.
examples.business: A company inside a company for a new product line.
examples.everyday: Store small bags inside a large bag.

principles.name: Anti-weight
subprinciples: Balance an object's weight by joining it with something that gives lift.
Balance weight with forces from the environment, such as air, water or magnetism.

examples.engineering: A counterweight on a lift or crane.
examples.software: Offset peak load with spare capacity that scales in when idle.
examples.business: Balance a seasonal business with a counter-seasonal product.
examples.everyday: Use a trolley so you do not carry the bags.

principles.name: Preliminary anti-action
subprinciples: If an action will have harmful effects too, counter them in advance.
Put stress into an object ahead of time that opposes the stress it will meet later.

examples.engineering: Pre-stressed concrete beams.
examples.software: Add rate limits before a launch to protect the database.
examples.business: Negotiate exit terms before signing a partnership.
examples.everyday: Take a vaccine before travelling.

principles.name: Preliminary action
subprinciples: Do the needed change, fully or in part, before it is needed.
Place objects in advance where they can act at once from the most convenient spot.

examples.engineering: Pre-glued wallpaper.
examples.software: Precompute and cache results before users ask.
examples.business: Write answers to common questions before customers ask them.
examples.everyday: Lay out clothes the night before.

principles.name: Beforehand cushioning
subprinciples: Make up for low reliability with emergency measures prepared in advance.

examples.engineering: A parachute with a reserve chute.
examples.software: Automatic failover to a standby replica; backups.
examples.business: A cash reserve for a bad quarter.
examples.everyday: Keep a spare key with a neighbour.

principles.name: Equipotentiality
subprinciples: Change working conditions so the object does not need to be raised or lowered.
Remove the need to fight a field or gradient by keeping things on one level.

examples.engineering: A mechanic's pit so the car does not need lifting.
examples.software: Keep services on the same version so no translation layer is needed.
examples.business: Flatten approval levels so requests do not move up and down the hierarchy.
examples.everyday: Keep the things you use daily at arm height.

principles.name: The other way round
subprinciples: Do the opposite of the usual action.
Make the moving part fixed and the fixed part moving.
Turn the object or process upside down.

examples.engineering: A treadmill: the floor moves, the runner stays.
examples.software: Push notifications instead of polling.
examples.business: Customers come to you instead of field sales visiting them.
examples.everyday: Bring the laundry basket to the wardrobe, not the clothes to the basket.

principles.name: Spheroidality
subprinciples: Use curves instead of straight lines, and spheres instead of cubes.
Use rollers, balls and spirals.
Switch from straight motion to rotation, or use centrifugal force.

examples.engineering: Arches and domes carry load better than flat roofs.
examples.software: A ring buffer instead of an ever-growing queue.
examples.business: Circular, repeat-purchase models instead of one-off sales.
examples.everyday: A round-edged table that nobody bumps into.

principles.name: Dynamics
subprinciples: Let the object or its environment adjust to work best at each stage.
Split the object into parts that can move relative to each other.
Make a rigid or fixed object movable or adaptable.

examples.engineering: Adjustable car seats and mirrors.
examples.software: Autoscaling; feature flags that change behaviour at runtime.
examples.business: Dynamic pricing.
examples.everyday: Adjustable shelves.

principles.name: Partial or excessive actions
aliases: do a little less or more
subprinciples: If exactly 100% is hard to get, do slightly less or slightly more and the problem may become easy.

examples.engineering: Overfill a mould, then trim the excess.
examples.software: Ship a rough first version, then refine.
examples.business: Overbook slightly to make up for no-shows.
examples.everyday: Buy a bit too much paint rather than run out mid-wall.

principles.name: Another dimension
subprinciples: Move from one dimension to two, or from two to three.
Stack objects in layers instead of one layer.
Tilt or turn the object on its side.
Use the other side of a surface.

examples.engineering: Multi-storey car parks; double-sided circuit boards.
examples.software: Add a second index; tag data instead of using one folder tree.
examples.business: Add a new axis of value, such as service on top of product.
examples.everyday: Wall-mounted storage.

principles.name: Mechanical vibration
subprinciples: Make an object vibrate or oscillate.
Raise the frequency, up to ultrasonic.
Use resonance or replace mechanical vibration with electric or piezo vibration.

examples.engineering: Vibrating concrete to remove air bubbles.
examples.software: Jitter on retries so clients do not hit the server at once.
examples.business: Short regular pulses of marketing instead of one big push.
examples.everyday: Shake a jar to settle its contents.

principles.name: Periodic action
subprinciples: Replace continuous action with periodic or pulsed action.
Change the frequency of a periodic action.
Use the pauses between pulses for another action.

examples.engineering: Pulsed welding; flashing warning lights.
examples.software: Batch jobs on a schedule instead of constant polling.
examples.business: Weekly check-ins instead of constant status updates.
examples.everyday: Interval training.

principles.name: Continuity of useful action
subprinciples: Keep all parts working at full load all the time.
Remove idle runs and interruptions.

examples.engineering: A continuous casting line instead of batch moulds.
examples.software: Streaming instead of nightly batches; CI that runs on every push.
examples.business: Follow-the-sun support across time zones.
examples.everyday: Listen to a podcast while commuting.

principles.name: Skipping
subprinciples: Run a harmful or hazardous step at very high speed.

examples.engineering: Cut plastic tubes fast so the heat cannot deform them.
examples.software: Run a risky migration in one short window rather than spread out.
examples.business: Rip off the bandage: announce bad news quickly and once.
examples.everyday: Pull off a plaster in one go.

principles.name: Blessing in disguise
subprinciples: Use a harmful factor to get a positive effect.
Remove a harmful factor by adding it to another harmful factor.
Increase a harmful factor until it stops being harmful.

examples.engineering: Waste heat from a power plant heats nearby homes.
examples.software: Turn error logs into a dashboard of what users actually try to do.
examples.business: Turn customer complaints into a public roadmap.
examples.everyday: Use a power cut as a reason for a candlelit dinner.

principles.name: Feedback
subprinciples: Add feedback to improve a process or action.
If there is feedback already, change its size or influence.

examples.engineering: A thermostat controlling a heater.
examples.software: Alerting on error rates; canary deploys that roll back on bad metrics.
examples.business: Net promoter surveys after each support case.
examples.everyday: A fitness tracker that nudges you to move.

principles.name: Intermediary
subprinciples: Use an in-between object to carry or transfer an action.
Join an object for a while to another one that is easy to remove.

examples.engineering: A drill guide that holds the bit at the right angle.
examples.software: An API gateway or message queue between services.
examples.business: A broker or agent between buyer and seller.
examples.everyday: Use a cutting board instead of cutting on the counter.

principles.name: Self-service
subprinciples: Let the object serve, maintain or repair itself.
Use waste material or energy the object already produces.

examples.engineering: Self-sharpening blades; regenerative braking.
examples.software: Self-healing services that restart on failure; auto-generated docs.
examples.business: Self-service help centre and checkout.
examples.everyday: A self-cleaning oven.

principles.name: Copying
subprinciples: Use a simple, cheap copy instead of an object that is unavailable, fragile or costly.
Replace an object with an optical copy or image, possibly scaled.
Move from visible copies to infrared or ultraviolet ones.

examples.engineering: Wind-tunnel tests on a scale model.
examples.software: Test against a staging copy or a mock instead of production.
examples.business: A pilot in one city before a national launch.
examples.everyday: Try furniture in your room with an AR app.

principles.name: Cheap short-living objects
subprinciples: Replace a costly object with several cheap ones, accepting shorter life.

examples.engineering: Disposable surgical instruments.
examples.software: Throwaway prototypes; ephemeral test environments.
examples.business: Short low-cost experiments instead of one big bet.
examples.everyday: Paper plates for a party.

principles.name: Mechanics substitution
subprinciples: Replace a mechanical system with an optical, acoustic, thermal or smell-based one.
Use electric, magnetic or electromagnetic fields to act on the object.
Move from fixed to changing fields, or from unstructured to structured ones.

examples.engineering: Touchless sensors instead of mechanical switches.
examples.software: Replace manual checks with automated monitors or rules.
examples.business: Replace paper forms with digital workflows.
examples.everyday: A motion-sensor light instead of a switch.

principles.name: Pneumatics and hydraulics
subprinciples: Use gas or liquid parts instead of solid ones: inflatable, liquid-filled, air-cushioned or hydraulic.

examples.engineering: Air bags; hydraulic lifts.
examples.software: Elastic resource pools that flow to where load is.
examples.business: Flexible staffing pools that move between teams.
examples.everyday: An inflatable mattress for guests.

principles.name: Flexible shells and thin films
subprinciples: Replace solid structures with flexible shells or thin films.
Isolate an object from its surroundings with a thin film.

examples.engineering: Shrink wrap; a thin protective coating.
examples.software: A thin adapter layer around a legacy system.
examples.business: A light brand shell around a white-label product.
examples.everyday: Cling film over a bowl.

principles.name: Porous materials
subprinciples: Make an object porous or add porous parts.
If it is already porous, fill the pores with something useful.

examples.engineering: Porous bearings filled with oil.
examples.software: Leave slack in the schedule that can absorb urgent work.
examples.business: Open, permeable team boundaries for knowledge flow.
examples.everyday: A sponge that holds soap.

principles.name: Color changes
subprinciples: Change the color of an object or its surroundings.
Change how transparent the object or its surroundings are.
Use colored additives or markers to see things that are hard to see.

examples.engineering: Temperature-sensitive paint that changes color when hot.
examples.software: Color-coded status and diff highlighting.
examples.business: Visual boards that show work state at a glance.
examples.everyday: Color-coded keys or folders.

principles.name: Homogeneity
subprinciples: Make objects that interact out of the same material, or a material with similar properties.

examples.engineering: A container made of the same material as its contents to avoid reactions.
examples.software: One language and toolchain across front end and back end.
examples.business: Shared values and vocabulary across merged teams.
examples.everyday: Use one brand of charger for all devices.

principles.name: Discarding and recovering
subprinciples: Let parts that have done their job go away (dissolve, evaporate, drop off) or change them while in use.
Restore used-up parts while the system runs.

examples.engineering: Dissolving capsules; rocket stages that drop off.
examples.software: Temporary scaffolding code removed after migration; garbage collection.
examples.business: Sunset products that served their purpose.
examples.everyday: Biodegradable plant pots that go into the soil.

principles.name: Parameter changes
subprinciples: Change the physical state, such as solid, liquid or gas.
Change concentration, consistency or density.
Change flexibility.
Change temperature or another property.

examples.engineering: Freeze liquids to transport them; concentrate juice.
examples.software: Change consistency levels; compress data; change cache TTL.
examples.business: Change pricing from one-off to subscription.
examples.everyday: Freeze leftovers to keep them longer.

principles.name: Phase transitions
subprinciples: Use effects that happen during a change of phase, such as change of volume or release or absorption of heat.

examples.engineering: Heat pipes that move heat by evaporation and condensation.
examples.software: Use the moment of a state change (deploy, failover) to run checks.
examples.business: Use a reorganisation as the moment to change habits.
examples.everyday: Ice packs that absorb heat as they melt.

principles.name: Thermal expansion
subprinciples: Use the expansion or contraction of materials with temperature.
Combine materials with different expansion rates.

examples.engineering: Bimetallic strips in thermostats.
examples.software: Capacity that grows with demand and shrinks after it.
examples.business: Teams that grow and shrink with the project phase.
examples.everyday: Run a stuck jar lid under hot water.

principles.name: Strong oxidants
subprinciples: Replace normal air with enriched air, enriched air with oxygen, and so on, to speed up a process.
Use a more active environment or agent.

examples.engineering: Oxygen-enriched combustion for higher temperatures.
examples.software: Run critical jobs on dedicated, faster hardware.
examples.business: Put a small tiger team on an urgent project.
examples.everyday: Use a pressure cooker.

principles.name: Inert atmosphere
subprinciples: Replace the normal environment with an inert one.
Add neutral parts or inert additives to the object.

examples.engineering: Argon shielding gas in welding.
examples.software: Run tests in an isolated sandbox with no side effects.
examples.business: A quiet room or no-meeting day for focused work.
examples.everyday: Vacuum-sealed food bags.

principles.name: Composite materials
subprinciples: Replace a uniform material with a composite one.

examples.engineering: Carbon fibre in resin; reinforced concrete.
examples.software: Combine rules and machine learning in one decision system.
examples.business: Mixed teams of senior and junior staff.
examples.everyday: A layered outfit for changing weather.
